{{Short description|Theorem in mathematics}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Richards' theorem''' is a result due to [[Paul I. Richards]] in 1947.  The theorem states that for

:<math>R(s) = \frac{kZ(s)-sZ(k)}{kZ(k)-sZ(s)},</math>

if <math>Z(s)</math> is a [[positive-real function]] (PRF) then <math>R(s)</math> is a PRF for all [[real number|real]], positive values of <math>k</math>.<ref>Wing, p. 122</ref>

The theorem has applications in electrical [[network synthesis]].  The PRF property of an impedance function determines whether or not a passive network can be realised having that impedance.  Richards' theorem led to a new method of realising such networks in the 1940s.

== Proof ==

:<math>R(s) = \frac{kZ(s)-sZ(k)}{kZ(k)-sZ(s)}</math>

where <math>Z(s)</math> is a PRF, <math>k</math> is a positive real constant, and <math>s= \sigma + i \omega</math> is the [[complex frequency]] variable, can be written as,

:<math>R(s) = \dfrac{1-W(s)}{1+W(s)}</math>

where,

:<math>W(s) = {1 - \dfrac{Z(s)}{Z(k)} \over 1 + \dfrac{Z(s)}{Z(k)}} \left( \frac{k+s}{k-s} \right)</math>

Since <math>Z(s)</math> is PRF then

:<math>1 +  \dfrac{Z(s)}{Z(k)}</math>

is also PRF.  The [[zero (complex analysis)|zeroes]] of this function are the [[pole (complex analysis)|poles]] of <math>W(s)</math>.  Since a PRF can have no zeroes in the right-half [[s-plane|''s''-plane]], then <math>W(s)</math> can have no poles in the right-half ''s''-plane and hence is analytic in the right-half ''s''-plane.

Let

:<math>Z(i \omega) = r (\omega) + ix(\omega)</math>

Then the magnitude of <math>W(i \omega)</math> is given by, 

:<math>\left| W(i \omega) \right| = \sqrt{ \dfrac{ (Z(k) - r(\omega))^2 +x(\omega)^2 }{ (Z(k) + r(\omega))^2 +x(\omega)^2 }}</math>

Since the PRF condition requires that <math>r(\omega) \ge 0</math> for all <math>\omega</math> then <math>\left| W(i \omega) \right| \le 1</math> for all <math>\omega</math>.  The maximum magnitude of <math>W(s)</math> occurs on the <math>i \omega</math> axis because <math>W(s)</math> is analytic in the right-half ''s''-plane.  Thus <math>|W(s)| \le 1</math> for <math>\sigma \ge 0</math>.

Let <math>W(s) = u( \sigma, \omega) + iv( \sigma, \omega)</math>, then the real part of <math>R(s)</math> is given by,

:<math>\Re (R(s)) = \dfrac{1 - |W(s)|^2}{ (1 + u( \sigma, \omega))^2 + v^2(\sigma, \omega)}</math>

Because <math>W(s) \le 1</math> for <math>\sigma \ge 0</math> then <math>\Re (R(s)) \ge 0</math> for <math>\sigma \ge 0</math> and consequently <math>R(s)</math> must be a PRF.<ref>Wing, pp. 122–123</ref>

Richards' theorem can also be derived  from [[Schwarz's lemma]].<ref>Hubbard, p. 33</ref>

== Uses ==
The theorem was introduced by [[Paul I. Richards]] as part of his investigation into the properties of PRFs.  The term ''PRF'' was coined by [[Otto Brune]] who [[mathematical proof|proved]] that the PRF property was a [[necessary and sufficient]] condition for a function to be realisable as a passive [[electrical network]], an important result in [[network synthesis]].<ref>Cauer ''et al.'', pp. 6–7</ref>  Richards gave the theorem in his 1947 paper in the reduced form,<ref>Richards, p. 779</ref>

:<math>R(s) = \frac{Z(s)-sZ(1)}{Z(1)-sZ(s)}</math>

that is, the special case where <math>k=1</math>

The theorem (with the more general casse of <math>k</math> being able to take on any value) formed the basis of the [[network synthesis]] technique presented by [[Raoul Bott]] and [[Richard Duffin]] in 1949.<ref>Wing, p. 122</ref>  In the Bott-Duffin synthesis, <math>Z(s)</math> represents the electrical network to be synthesised and <math>R(s)</math> is another (unknown) network incorporated within it (<math>R(s)</math> is unitless, but <math>R(s)Z(k)</math> has units of impedance and <math>R(s)/Z(k)</math> has units of admittance).  Making <math>Z(s)</math> the subject gives

:<math>Z(s) = \left( \frac{R(s)}{Z(k)} + \frac{k}{sZ(k)} \right)^{-1} +  \left(\frac{1}{Z(k) R(s)} + \frac{s}{k Z(k)} \right)^{-1}</math>

Since <math>Z(k)</math> is merely a positive [[real number]], <math>Z(s)</math> can be synthesised as a new network proportional to <math>R(s)</math> in parallel with a capacitor all in series with a network proportional to the inverse of <math>R(s)</math> in parallel with an inductor.  By a suitable choice for the value of <math>k</math>, a resonant circuit can be extracted from <math>R(s)</math> leaving a function <math>Z'(s)</math> two degrees lower than <math>Z(s)</math>.  The whole process can then be applied iteratively to <math>Z'(s)</math> until the degree of the function is reduced to something that can be realised directly.<ref>{{multiref|Wing, pp. 123–125|Hughes ''et al.'', pp. 284–285}}</ref>

The advantage of the Bott-Duffin synthesis is that, unlike other methods, it is able to synthesise any PRF.  Other methods have limitations such as only being able to deal with two kinds of [[electrical element|element]] in any single network.  Its major disadvantage is that it does not result in the minimal number of elements in a network.  The number of elements grows exponentially with each iteration.  After the first iteration there are two <math>Z'</math> and associated elements, after the second, there are four <math>Z''</math> and so on.<ref>Wing, p. 115</ref>

Hubbard notes that Bott and Duffin appeared not to know the relationship of Richards' theorem to Schwarz's lemma and offers it as his own discovery,<ref>Hubbard, p. 33</ref> but it was certainly known to Richards who used it in his own proof of the theorem.<ref>Richards, p. 779</ref>
